parts.label: a
hints: Recall the formulas for the mean and variance of a binomial distribution: $\mu = np$ and $\sigma^2 = np(1-p)$.
Substitute $n = 200$, $p = 0.8$, and $q = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2$ into both formulas.

walkthrough.text:
Use the formula for the mean of a binomial distribution:
$$\mu = np = 200 \times 0.8 = 160$$

Use the formula for the variance of a binomial distribution:
$$\sigma^2 = np(1 - p) = 200 \times 0.8 \times 0.2 = 32$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Calculate the expected value directly:
$$\mu = np = 200(0.8) = 160$$

Calculate the variance using $q = 1 - p$:
$$\sigma^2 = npq = 200(0.8)(0.2) = 32$$

ai_rubric.observable: Calculate mean mu = n*p = 200 * 0.8 = 160.
Calculate variance sigma^2 = n*p*(1 - p) = 200 * 0.8 * 0.2 = 32.

parts.label: a
hints: Calculate both expected successes $np$ and expected failures $nq = n(1-p)$.

walkthrough.text:

$$90 > 5 \quad \text{and} \quad 60 > 5$$
Since both $np > 5$ and $nq > 5$, the conditions for a normal approximation are satisfied.

teacher_walkthrough.text:

$$np = 90 > 5 \quad \text{and} \quad nq = 60 > 5$$

parts.label: a
hints: The conditions for a normal approximation are $np > 5$ and $nq > 5$.
Because $p = 0.04 < 0.5$, $np < nq$, so $np > 5$ is the restrictive inequality.
Substitute $p = 0.04$ into $np > 5$ and solve for $n$.
Since $n$ must be an integer strictly greater than 125, choose the smallest possible integer.

walkthrough.text:
Identify the more restrictive condition since $p = 0.04 < q = 0.96$:
$$np > 5$$

Substitute $p = 0.04$ and solve the inequality for $n$:
$$0.04n > 5 \implies n > \frac{5}{0.04} = 125$$

Select the smallest integer strictly satisfying $n > 125$:
$$n = 126$$
(Note: $nq = 126 \times 0.96 = 120.96 > 5$ is automatically satisfied.)

ai_rubric.observable: Set up the restrictive condition np > 5 using p = 0.04: n * 0.04 > 5.
Solve the inequality to obtain n > 125.
Conclude that the smallest integer is n = 126.

parts.label: c
hints: Consider what $npq$ represents: it is the variance, measuring the spread of the distribution.
Think about what happens to the shape of a binomial distribution when $p$ is very close to 0 or 1.
Even if $npq > 5$, one of the expected values ($np$ or $nq$) could still be too close to a boundary (0 or $n$).
Boundary proximity causes severe skewness, whereas the normal distribution is symmetric.
State clearly why both separate conditions $np > 5$ and $nq > 5$ are required.

walkthrough.text:
Explain the role of $npq$:
$$\sigma^2 = npq$$
The quantity $npq$ measures only the variance (spread) of the distribution, not whether the distribution is reasonably symmetric.

Analyze the effect of extreme probabilities:
$$\text{Skewness} = \frac{q - p}{\sqrt{npq}}$$
When $p$ is close to 0 (or 1), the binomial distribution remains heavily skewed unless $n$ is very large.

Explain boundary effects:
$$X \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}$$
If only $npq > 5$ were checked, expected values close to 0 or $n$ could cause severe truncation at the boundaries.

State why the separate conditions are essential:
$$np > 5 \quad \text{and} \quad nq > 5$$
Both conditions ensure that the mean is sufficiently far from both boundaries (0 and $n$), guaranteeing the symmetry required for a normal approximation.

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Address variance vs symmetry:
$$\sigma^2 = npq$$
The variance $npq > 5$ ensures spread, but does not guarantee symmetry.

Discuss skewness when $p$ is near 0 or 1:
$$\text{If } p \to 0, \text{ skewness is high}$$

State why both conditions are required:
$$np > 5 \quad \text{and} \quad nq > 5$$
Both $np > 5$ and $nq > 5$ ensure the distribution is far enough from endpoints 0 and $n$ to resemble a symmetric bell curve.

ai_rubric.observable: Explain that npq measures spread (variance) but does not ensure that both tails are far enough from 0 and n.
State that when p is very close to 0 or 1, the binomial distribution is highly skewed.
Conclude that both np > 5 and nq > 5 are necessary to ensure sufficient symmetry and avoid truncation at the boundaries.
